## Overview: Frequency of Cholecystectomy

- Cholecystectomy is one of the most frequently performed general surgery procedures in the United States
- Over 500,000 procedures are performed annually
- Reasons include the frequency of gallbladder disease and indications for intervention in the US population

---

## Overview: Rise of Laparoscopic Approach

- The advent of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the 1980s resulted in a rapid rise in the number of cholecystectomies
- Benefits include reduced postoperative recovery, reduced pain, and ability to complete the procedure in the outpatient setting
- As familiarity with laparoscopy has increased, the incidence of open cholecystectomy has steadily decreased

---

## Overview: Chapter Scope

- This chapter addresses techniques of open cholecystectomy because this approach is still used when laparoscopy is contraindicated or technically impossible
- Appropriate laparoscopic cholecystectomy techniques will be discussed
- Strategies to prevent common bile duct injuries (CBDI) will be covered
- Alternative minimally invasive approaches and common complications will also be addressed

---

## Indications: Symptomatic Gallstones

- Symptomatic gallstones are the primary reason a patient requires cholecystectomy
- In the US, approximately 5% to 22% of the population has cholelithiasis
- Cholelithiasis can lead to several pathologic conditions including biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, gallstone pancreatitis, or choledocholithiasis

---

## Indications: Asymptomatic Gallstones

- The majority of patients with cholelithiasis will remain asymptomatic
- Prophylactic cholecystectomy in asymptomatic patients is typically not warranted
- Cholecystectomy may be indicated for certain populations with asymptomatic cholelithiasis
- Example: sickle cell anemia where hepatic and vaso-occlusive disease can be indistinguishable from acute biliary pathology

---

## Indications: Gallbladder Polyps

- Gallbladder polyps without cholelithiasis can be an indication for cholecystectomy
- Resection is recommended for gallbladder polyps greater than or equal to 10 mm
- Resection is also recommended in patients with biliary symptoms in the setting of gallbladder polyps of any size

---

## Indications: Concomitant Procedures

- Cholecystectomy is often performed concomitantly with other procedures
- Examples include pancreaticoduodenectomy and major anatomic liver resections
- Cholecystectomy at the time of bariatric surgery is controversial
- It is thought that biliary symptoms increase after extreme weight loss

---

## Indications: Bariatric Surgery Considerations

- A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that concomitant cholecystectomy increases postoperative morbidity and operative time
- The decision to perform concomitant cholecystectomy during bariatric surgery requires careful consideration of risks and benefits

---

## Indications: Timing of Cholecystectomy

- Timing of cholecystectomy can vary by indication
- Acute cholecystitis cases should proceed to the operating room as early as possible
- A recent study using a Swedish registry found that adverse events, mortality, and CBDIs were higher in patients who underwent cholecystectomy more than 4 days after admission

---

## Indications: Optimal Timing for Acute Cholecystitis

- Data suggest the optimal timing for cholecystectomy is within 48 hours of admission for acute cholecystitis
- Delayed surgery beyond this window is associated with worse outcomes
- Early intervention remains the standard of care

---

## Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Standard of Care

- Laparoscopy has become the standard access for removing the gallbladder
- Multiple studies have shown a decrease in postoperative pain
- Earlier return to normal activity compared to open cholecystectomy
- Decrease in hospital length of stay (LOS)
- Reduction in incisional hernia development

---

## Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Anatomical Knowledge

- Familiarity with the anatomy of the porta hepatis is essential
- Knowledge of common biliary and vascular variations can reduce complication rates
- This is particularly important for challenging cases presenting with significant inflammation

---

## Operating Room Setup: Equipment Verification

- Before beginning any procedure, the surgeon must ensure that all equipment is present and functional
- This includes equipment for potentially necessary procedures such as cholangiography
- Equipment for potential conversion to laparotomy must also be available

---

## Box 36.1: Equipment for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy

- Comprehensive equipment list is essential for safe laparoscopic cholecystectomy
- Equipment is divided into categories: viewing equipment, dissection instruments, and instruments for unusual circumstances
- Proper preparation prevents intraoperative delays and complications

---

## Box 36.1: Laparoscopic Viewing Equipment

- Camera light source
- Laparoscope (5-mm and 10-mm, 30-degree)
- Monitors (one over each shoulder)
- Insufflator and tubing
- Trocars (multiple 5-mm trocars and at least one 10-mm)

---

## Box 36.1: Instruments for Dissection and Removal

- Clips (5-mm and 10-mm variety)
- Electrocautery
- Suction and irrigation
- Atraumatic graspers
- Maryland grasper (or laparoscopic right angle grasper)
- Endoscopic retrieval bag

---

## Box 36.1: Instruments for Unusual Circumstances

- Endoloop
- Laparoscopic needle driver
- Absorbable hemostatic agent
- Staplers
- Argon laser
- Cholangiography equipment (catheter, injectable contrast, C-arm for fluoroscopy)
- Open cholecystectomy tray and instruments

---

## Port Placement and Exposure: Initial Access

- Once pneumoperitoneum is obtained, a 5- or 10-mm port is placed in the periumbilical region
- A 30-degree laparoscope is inserted
- The abdominal cavity is inspected systematically

---

## Port Placement and Exposure: Trocar Positions

- One 5-mm trocar is placed along the right anterior axillary line 2 centimeters below the costal margin
- The other 5-mm port is placed at the midclavicular line on the right at the edge of the liver
- A fourth port (5- or 10-mm) is placed in the subxiphoid region

---

## Port Placement and Exposure: Subxiphoid Port

- The subxiphoid port should be placed 2 to 4 centimeters below the xiphoid
- Exact placement depends on the location of the gallbladder and falciform ligament
- A fifth port can be placed in the location deemed most appropriate for additional retraction if needed

---

## Figure 36.1: Trocar Positions

- **Panel A**: Positions for insertion of trocars during laparoscopic cholecystectomy
  - Laparoscope (A) is positioned in the periumbilical region
  - Graspers for gallbladder retraction (B) and manipulation (C) are positioned in the right upper quadrant along the subcostal region
  - Subxyphoid region (D) is used for the dissector, diathermy, and clip appliers
- **Panel B**: Cross-sectional view showing gallbladder, liver, and laparoscope positioning

---

## Dissection and Critical View of Safety: Initial Retraction

- An atraumatic grasper is placed through the most lateral port
- The fundus of the gallbladder is grasped to retract it cephalad and laterally
- This raises the liver edge and exposes the neck of the gallbladder and the porta

---

## Dissection and Critical View of Safety: Infundibulum Manipulation

- With the gallbladder retracted cephalad, a second atraumatic grasper is placed through the midclavicular port
- This grasper manipulates the infundibulum of the gallbladder
- Adhesions should be taken down until the gallbladder infundibulum can be seen clearly

---

## Dissection and Critical View of Safety: Triangle of Calot

- Retraction of the infundibulum caudally and to the right exposes the triangle of Calot
- A cautery instrument placed through the xiphoid port opens the peritoneum in the triangle of Calot
- Dissection should be started at the edge of the gallbladder neck to avoid iatrogenic injury to aberrant hepatic vasculature or bile ducts

---

## Dissection and Critical View of Safety: Peritoneal Dissection

- Dissection of the peritoneum is continued on both sides of the gallbladder
- Stay 1 to 2 mm from the liver edge
- Attention is next turned to obtaining the critical view of safety (CVS)

---

## Critical View of Safety: Importance

- The CVS technique has been shown to reduce the rates of iatrogenic bile duct injuries
- A recent multisociety consensus statement recommended CVS for identification of the cystic duct and cystic artery during laparoscopic cholecystectomy
- When CVS was not attainable, a subtotal cholecystectomy should be performed rather than attempting a fundus-first approach

---

## Critical View of Safety: Dissection Technique

- Attachments at the neck of the gallbladder are dissected using a combination of blunt and cautery assisted dissection
- It is useful to serially retract the infundibulum medially and laterally to fully dissect the triangle of Calot
- Carrying dissection to the level of the common bile duct (CBD) is not indicated because this only increases the risk for iatrogenic injury

---

## Critical View of Safety: Creating the Window

- Blunt dissection with a Maryland grasper or right-angle grasper can help create a window behind the cystic duct
- Spread in the avascular tissue
- The gallbladder is dissected off the liver edge, exposing the cystic plate

---

## Box 36.2: Doublet Scoring for Critical View of Safety

- Criteria for Achieving Critical View of Safety:
  1. Two structures connected to gallbladder: Only two structures clearly seen entering the gallbladder
  2. Cystic plate: Approximately 1/3 of cystic plate is clearly visible
  3. Clearance of hepatocystic triangle: Hepatocystic triangle is cleared of tissue so visibility of cystic structures and plate is unimpeded

---

## Box 36.2: Certainty of Anatomy

- The surgeon must be certain no other structures are in the hepatocystic triangle
- If any question or doubt about the anatomy is encountered, a cholangiogram should be performed to reorient the surgeon
- These views are demonstrated in Figure 36.3

---

## Figure 36.2: Anatomical Triangles

- **Panel A**: Triangle of cholecystectomy limited by the common hepatic duct, right hepatic duct, cystic duct, and inferior liver edge
- **Panel B**: The triangle of Calot limited by the common hepatic duct, cystic duct, and cystic artery
- Understanding these boundaries is essential for safe dissection

---

## Figure 36.3: Critical View of Safety

- **Panel A (Anterior view)**: Hepatocystic triangle is dissected free of all tissue except for the cystic duct and artery, and one-third of the cystic plate on the liver bed is exposed
- **Panel B (Posterior view)**: Critical view of safety during laparoscopic cholecystectomy showing posterior perspective
- When this view is achieved, the two structures entering the gallbladder can only be the cystic duct and artery

---

## CVS Achievement in Practice

- Most surgeons attempt the CVS during laparoscopic cholecystectomy
- In practice, it is rarely achieved properly
- An evaluation of 160 online videos of laparoscopic cholecystectomy found only one video accomplished a passing CVS score

---

## Safe Cholecystectomy Curriculum

- The safe cholecystectomy curriculum can be found free of charge at the Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons (SAGES) website
- Education and training on CVS are essential for reducing bile duct injuries
- Continuous quality improvement is needed in this area

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Clipping Structures

- Once all critical anatomy is confirmed, the cystic artery and duct are clipped and divided
- Care should be taken to avoid tenting the CBD with clips placed too distally on the cystic duct
- The tips of the clip should be directly visualized to be free before closing

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Clip Safety

- Avoid inadvertent injury to other structures
- Ensure the clip completely occludes the artery or duct
- If it is not possible to secure a clip completely across a structure, an Endoloop device can be used to ligate it

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Division

- Scissors are used to divide the cystic artery and duct
- In rare cases with a large inflamed cystic duct that cannot accommodate clips, endovascular staplers can be used to divide and secure the duct
- Cautery is avoided for division because of the increased risk for necrosis resulting in clip slippage

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Gallbladder Dissection

- The gallbladder is dissected off the cystic plate from the infundibulum to the fundus with electrocautery
- Blindly placing clips, clamps, or cauterizing at this time risks causing hemorrhage
- Risk of inadvertent injury to the hepatic blood supply, superficial biliary pedicles, or middle hepatic vein branches

---

## Figure 36.4: Risks of Blind Clip Placement

- Blind placement of clips or clamps for hemostasis can result in injury to the hepatic artery or bile ducts
- Four panels demonstrate potential injuries to various ductal and vascular structures
- Proper visualization is essential before placing any clips in the hepatocystic triangle

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Inspection

- Before completely freeing the gallbladder from the liver, the gallbladder is used for retraction
- Inspect the cystic plate for hemostasis
- Inspect that clips are still securely placed on the cystic duct and artery

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Specimen Removal

- Specimen removal is performed through the periumbilical incision
- This incision is easy to enlarge to extract large gallstones
- Bag extraction is performed with videoscopic visualization to ensure the bag does not rip and specimen contents are not lost

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Irrigation and Closure

- Spilled bile or debris should be completely irrigated and cleared with suction
- This prevents subsequent migration or abscess formation
- The fascia of port sites greater than 10 mm are closed to prevent development of incisional hernias

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy: Fascial Closure

- Some surgeons elect not to close the epigastric site because herniation is unlikely in that location
- Proper closure technique depends on port size and location
- Attention to fascial closure prevents long-term complications

---

## Three-Port and Two-Port Techniques: Rationale

- Attempts to improve on the traditional four-port laparoscopic cholecystectomy by decreasing the number of port sites have been introduced
- Proponents cite reduced cost related to fewer trocars, fewer scars, and reduced cost
- The series reporting these techniques are small but suggest that these techniques are feasible and safe

---

## Three-Port and Two-Port Techniques: Method

- Typically, the right upper quadrant ports are eliminated by using suture to retract the gallbladder in their stead
- Modified techniques have been described for two-port laparoscopic cholecystectomy
- These approaches require advanced laparoscopic skills

---

## Three-Port and Two-Port Techniques: Evidence

- A small randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 217 patients compared four-port with three-port cholecystectomy
- Found no difference in length of operation or morbidity, including iatrogenic bile duct injuries
- However, there was also no difference in pain medication required between groups

---

## Three-Port and Two-Port Techniques: Current Status

- Currently, there are no obvious advantages that these techniques offer over the four-port approach
- The standard four-port technique remains the gold standard
- Reduced port techniques may be considered in select circumstances

---

## Single-Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Introduction

- Single-incision laparoscopic cholecystectomy (SILC) is the extreme attempt at reducing the number of ports
- SILC is performed through a single transabdominal incision, usually at the umbilicus
- There are specifically designed single-port systems and instruments available that have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration

---

## Single-Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Evidence

- Several RCTs comparing SILC with standard laparoscopic cholecystectomy have been performed
- Most are hampered by low accrual
- A 2017 trial from Egypt enrolled 187 patients

---

## Single-Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Results

- SILC had a statistically significant longer operating time and conversion rate compared with three-port laparoscopic cholecystectomy
- The only advantage to SILC in this study was the aesthetic score
- In addition to the absence of benefit to the patient, SILC induces significantly more stress on the surgeon

---

## Single-Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Surgeon Stress

- A double-blind RCT measured surgeon heart rate and salivary cortisol
- Measured before being randomized, after clipping the cystic duct, and while closing skin
- SILC was associated with higher heart rates and cortisol levels
- Surgeons also reported the surgical workload was more demanding with SILC

---

## Single-Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Patient Selection

- Careful patient selection is necessary to optimize the use of this technique
- It is critical to understand that the CVS should be obtained regardless of the number of laparoscopic ports used
- This reduces the risk of vasculobiliary injury during minimally invasive cholecystectomy

---

## Robotic-Assisted Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Introduction

- The use of robotic assisted laparoscopic surgery has significantly increased in recent years
- This upswing is because of a combination of aggressive marketing resulting in patient demand
- The platform is attractive to surgeons as well

---

## Robotic-Assisted Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Advantages

- Offers the benefits of 3-dimensional (3D) visualization
- Improved ergonomics
- An easier learning curve compared with laparoscopy
- Robotic laparoscopic cholecystectomy has been proposed as an ideal tool to improve skill and confidence using the robotic platform

---

## Robotic-Assisted Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Costs

- Despite similar outcomes, robotic surgery is associated with significantly higher costs than laparoscopy
- The upfront cost of purchasing a robotic console is approximately 2 million dollars
- There is also the cost of maintenance and replacement of disposable instruments

---

## Robotic-Assisted Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Outcomes

- A single institution analysis reported lower readmission rates with robotic cholecystectomy in propensity matched patients
- However, the overall hospital costs and operative time were significantly larger
- These cost discrepancies must be considered when deciding on the optimal minimally invasive approach

---

## Contraindications: Categories

- Contraindications to this procedure are divided into two categories:
  1. Contraindications to cholecystectomy
  2. Contraindications to laparoscopy

---

## Absolute Contraindications

- Absolute contraindications to operative cholecystectomy include:
  - Refractory coagulopathy
  - Intolerance of general anesthesia
- The 2018 Tokyo Guidelines do not discourage cholecystectomy for patients with severe sepsis and end-organ failure (Grade III cholecystitis) if supportive care is available and the operating surgeon feels the patient can withstand the procedure

---

## Relative Contraindications

- Relative contraindications include:
  - Severe cardiopulmonary disease
  - Pregnancy
  - Cirrhosis with portal hypertension
- Ultimately the decision is made based on clinical judgment

---

## Contraindications: Cirrhosis

- The presence of cirrhosis can complicate many abdominal surgical interventions
- Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in cirrhotic patients is especially challenging
- It can be difficult to retract the stiff, friable liver
- There is potential for bleeding from the associated coagulopathy

---

## Contraindications: Cirrhosis Outcomes

- Outcomes between Childs-Pugh A/B cirrhotic patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy and those with normal liver function are similar
- Exceptions include longer operative times
- There is a trend towards increased rates of conversion to open cholecystectomy in cirrhotic patients

---

## Contraindications: Portal Hypertension

- Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is also feasible in cirrhotics with portal hypertension
- The surgeon must be aware of aberrant portosystemic venous collateralization in the liver bed, porta hepatis, and abdominal wall
- An energy-sealing device should be available to limit blood loss during dissection

---

## Contraindications: Hemostasis in Cirrhosis

- Hemostatic agents and argon beam should be readily available to assist with hemostasis
- The procedure should be converted to an open procedure for significant bleeding that cannot be controlled laparoscopically
- Careful preoperative planning is essential in this population

---

## Conversion to Open: Overview

- Although laparoscopy is the preferred approach for cholecystectomy, there are many situations that may necessitate conversion to open procedure
- The decision and timing of intraoperative conversion to laparotomy depends on:
  - The surgeon's experience
  - Comfort with laparoscopic and open techniques
  - Patient factors (anatomy and pathology)

---

## Conversion to Open: Decision Making

- There is no consensus on when conversion is necessary as long as patient safety is the ultimate priority
- Contemporary conversion rates are reported to be between 5% to 10%
- Conversion has been described as a "complication" of laparoscopy by some

---

## Conversion to Open: Mature Judgment

- The view that conversion is a complication is untenable
- Conversion should be regarded as mature judgment because it can prevent disastrous complications in challenging cases
- Knowing when to convert is a critical surgical skill

---

## Conversion to Open: Indications

- Reasons to consider conversion include:
  - Unclear anatomy despite cholangiography
  - Intraoperative complication
  - Failure to progress
  - Pathology not amenable to laparoscopic or postoperative endoscopic techniques

---

## Conversion to Open: Risk Factors

- Independent factors associated with conversion to open cholecystectomy include:
  - Prior upper abdominal surgery
  - Pericholecystic fluid
  - Acute cholecystitis
  - Emergent cholecystectomy
- These factors should be considered during preoperative planning

---

## Open Technique: Incision

- The traditional incision used for an open cholecystectomy is a right subcostal or Kocher incision
- This incision is created 2 centimeters below the right costal margin
- It extends from the midline to the lateral edge of the right rectus muscle
- This incision can be extended superiorly along the midline if further exposure is needed

---

## Open Technique: Retrograde Cholecystectomy

- When performing a retrograde cholecystectomy, the critical view of safety must be identified before removing the gallbladder from the liver
- Although this is the usual approach during laparoscopic cholecystectomy, it can be more difficult for an inexperienced surgeon without the magnification of laparoscopy and difference in exposure
- The same principles must be maintained to prevent inadvertent biliary injury

---

## Open Technique: Retrograde Exposure

- The fundus of the gallbladder is grasped with a Kelly or similar clamp
- Peritoneum overlying the infundibulum is incised
- The incision is extended along the anterior and posterior gallbladder, being careful to stay close to the edge of the gallbladder

---

## Open Technique: Cystic Duct Identification

- Once the cystic duct is identified, a suture ligature is passed around it
- This is used to place tension on the duct for better exposure
- It also helps prevent stone migration into the CBD
- The CVS has been achieved once all fibroadipose tissue is cleared from the hepatocystic triangle

---

## Open Technique: CVS Criteria in Open Surgery

- Only two structures are seen clearly entering the gallbladder
- A third of the cystic plate is seen
- Any stones palpated within the cystic duct are "milked" back into the gallbladder
- The cystic artery can be ligated with either clips or sutures then divided

---

## Open Technique: Cholangiography and Duct Ligation

- If cholangiography is indicated, it is performed at this time
- Ligation and division of the cystic duct occurs after confirmation of anatomy
- The cystic duct should be ligated securely to prevent bile leakage

---

## Open Technique: Gallbladder Dissection from Liver

- To complete the retrograde cholecystectomy, the gallbladder is dissected off the cystic plate using cautery
- The dissection plane is kept close to the gallbladder to avoid entering the cystic plate and deeper liver parenchyma
- Brisk bleeding from liver parenchyma lacerations tend to be venous in nature

---

## Open Technique: Hepatic Vein Branches

- Distal branches of the middle hepatic vein can be located immediately deep to the cystic plate
- These can usually be treated by holding constant pressure over the area for 5 to 10 minutes
- Hemostatic agents may be beneficial in these instances as well

---

## Open Technique: Deep Hemostasis

- If pressure and hemostatic agents fail, deep hemostatic sutures can be placed
- One must be aware of the location of the right portal pedicle and its anterior branch
- These structures can be close to the base of the gallbladder

---

## Open Technique: Antegrade Cholecystectomy

- Antegrade cholecystectomy is an alternate technique for cholecystectomy
- This technique should not be used in the presence of severe inflammation that obstructs visualization of the cystic duct
- As with the fundus-down laparoscopic technique, there is still significant risk of biliary injury in these cases without proper visualization

---

## Open Technique: Antegrade Method

- A clamp is used to grasp the fundus of the gallbladder
- Another clamp is used to grasp the peritoneum on the liver edge to provide countertraction
- An incision is made in the gallbladder serosa approximately 5 millimeters from the liver edge with cautery

---

## Open Technique: Antegrade Dissection

- A dissection plane is developed between the superior gallbladder wall and the cystic plate
- Care is taken to avoid entering the cystic plate and lacerating the liver parenchyma
- This plane is continued medially and laterally toward the gallbladder neck
- An energy-sealing device can be used on edematous or vascularized peritoneum

---

## Open Technique: Antegrade Completion

- Dissection is performed posterior and lateral to fully free the gallbladder from the cystic plate
- This best exposes the cystic artery and duct
- The cystic artery is ligated and transected as it enters the gallbladder wall
- The infundibulum is dissected free to expose the cystic duct

---

## Open Technique: Antegrade Duct Management

- One should not dissect more than 1 centimeter of the cystic duct because this increases risk of CBDI
- Once the cystic duct is visualized, it can be ligated with suture or clips and divided
- The gallbladder is removed, and the abdomen is closed

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Introduction

- Subtotal cholecystectomy is the recommended technique for treating severely inflamed gallbladders when the CVS cannot be safely obtained
- Fibrosis and inflammation can cause the cystic duct to shorten and fuse with the CBD
- This can lead to the surgeon mistaking the CBD for the cystic duct

---

## Figure 36.5: CBD Misidentification

- The common hepatic duct can be mistaken for the cystic duct when the region of the infundibulum cannot be delineated because of fibrosis and inflammation
- This figure demonstrates the dangerous anatomical distortion that can occur in severe cholecystitis
- Recognition of this situation is critical for safe surgical decision-making

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Safety Principle

- In these cases, it is best to err on the side of caution and avoid dissecting in the hepatocystic triangle
- Cholecystitis can be managed safely until inflammation has subsided
- CBDIs have significant long-term morbidity

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Procedure Choice

- A partial or subtotal cholecystectomy, in which a portion of the gallbladder is removed and gallstones are extracted while leaving the posterior wall of the gallbladder in place, is the procedure of choice
- This provides source control and surgical drainage
- This technique can be used either open or laparoscopically

---

## Figure 36.6: Line of Safety

- The limit of proximal dissection for subtotal cholecystectomy is the "line of safety" between the sulcus of Rouviere and hilar plate
- This ensures dissection occurs away from the common bile duct in the setting of severe inflammation
- Key landmarks: Sulcus of Rouviere, Hilar plate, Line of safety

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Technique

- To perform a safe subtotal cholecystectomy, all dissection should be performed above the "line of safety"
- The gallbladder is drained and opened with cautery at the fundus
- Bile, stones, and debris are suctioned or set aside for future extraction in a specimen bag in a laparoscopic approach

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Incision Extension

- This incision is extended to the gallbladder neck without dissecting the cystic duct or artery
- The anterior wall of the gallbladder is then completely removed
- The posterior wall is left on the cystic plate

---

## Figure 36.7: Subtotal Cholecystectomy

- **Panel A**: Laparoscopic subtotal cholecystectomy demonstrating the anterior wall excised and a small strip of the posterior wall left attached to the liver
- **Panel B**: Open subtotal cholecystectomy showing the same principle
- The remnant mucosa can then be either removed or coagulated with cautery or argon beam

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Mucosal Management

- The remnant mucosa is then coagulated with either cautery or argon beam
- A drain should be placed near the gallbladder stump to drain potential bile leaks
- This is an essential step in preventing postoperative collections

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Trends

- Subtotal cholecystectomies, both open and laparoscopic, are being performed more frequently
- Conversion to open procedure is becoming less common
- Surgeons are becoming more comfortable with this technique as a safe alternative

---

## Partial or Subtotal Cholecystectomy: Complications

- As one may expect, there is a higher risk of bile leaks and subphrenic collection with subtotal cholecystectomy compared with standard cholecystectomy
- One study found the relative risk of bile leak after subtotal cholecystectomy was as high as 3-fold
- These were more common if the gallbladder remnant was left in situ

---

## Anatomic Variations: Introduction

- An intimate knowledge of gallbladder and biliary anatomy, as well as common variations, is essential to perform a safe cholecystectomy
- Variations in gallbladder anatomy such as duplicated, left-sided, bilobed, or congenitally absent gallbladder are rare
- They are typically identified preoperatively

---

## Anatomic Variations: Biliary Duct Variations

- Significant variations of the cystic duct and hepatic duct junction exist
- The common hepatic duct can range in length from 1 to 7.5 centimeters
- A large series of magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatographies demonstrated that 40.7% of patients had some variant in biliary tree anatomy

---

## Figure 36.8: Cystic Duct Variations

- **Panel A**: Variations in the confluence of the cystic duct and common hepatic duct
  - Multiple configurations of cystic duct insertion are shown
  - Low insertion, high insertion, parallel course, and spiral configurations
- **Panel B**: High insertion of the cystic duct demonstrated on endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography

---

## Anatomic Variations: Medial Insertion

- In this study, 5% of subjects had medial cystic duct insertion
- Anomalous extrahepatic bile ducts occur in up to 12% of patients
- The most common being an anomalous right sectoral duct that empties into either the common hepatic or cystic duct

---

## Figure 36.9: Right Sectoral Duct Variations

- **Panel A**: Variations in the confluence of the extrahepatic bile ducts and cystic duct
  - Six different configurations of right sectoral duct anatomy
  - These variations represent the only biliary drainage for the corresponding segment(s) of the liver
- **Panel B**: Cholangiogram demonstrating a cystic duct inserting into the right anterior section bile duct

---

## Anatomic Variations: Clinical Significance

- When these variations occur, they often represent the only biliary drainage for the corresponding segment(s) of the liver
- Thus injury or obstruction of these ducts results in liver atrophy or obstructive cholangitis in that segment
- True duplication of the cystic duct is exceedingly rare

---

## Anatomic Variations: Cholangiography Recommendation

- Cholangiography should be performed if the surgeon believes a true duplication or other significant anomaly has been encountered
- Preoperative imaging with MRCP can help identify these variations
- Intraoperative vigilance is essential when anatomy appears unusual

---

## Anatomic Variations: Arterial Anatomy

- Arterial anatomic variations are also common and can contribute to morbidity after cholecystectomy
- Typically, the cystic artery originates from the right hepatic artery (76%)
- It may also branch off the left, common, or proper hepatic arteries

---

## Anatomic Variations: Vasculobiliary Injury

- Arterial injury may accompany a bile duct injury resulting in a combined vasculobiliary injury
- The right hepatic artery is involved in 92% of these injuries because of its proximity to the CBD
- This can significantly add to the difficulty of bile duct repair

---

## Postoperative Management: Discharge

- Most patients undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy are discharged the same day
- This is because of the decreased pain profile associated with this minimally invasive technique
- A patient admitted with acute cholecystitis is often observed in the hospital overnight postoperatively because of infectious concerns

---

## Postoperative Management: Admission Criteria

- Elderly patients may benefit from postoperative admission
- Comorbid patients require closer monitoring
- Patients requiring significant analgesia postoperatively
- Patients with complicated procedures

---

## Postoperative Management: Diet and Pain Control

- The patient is allowed a diet shortly after surgery
- Oral narcotics for postoperative incisional pain can be prescribed for pain control
- Many patients recover with only over-the-counter pain medications, including nonsteroidal antiinflammatories and acetaminophen

---

## Postoperative Management: Follow-Up

- Routine follow-up by the surgeon in clinic can occur between 1 and 4 weeks after surgery
- Earlier follow-up may be needed for patients with complications or concerns
- Telephone follow-up may be appropriate for uncomplicated cases

---

## Immediate Postoperative Complications: Biliary Injury

- Biliary injury remains the most feared complication of cholecystectomy
- It has been shown that bile duct injuries have a 30-day mortality rate of 2% in a large database study
- Another prospective cohort of 800 patients with CBDI referred to a single center reported the mean survival after iatrogenic biliary injury was 17.6 years

---

## Biliary Injury: Long-Term Impact

- Patients with biliary injury had a worse physical quality of life and loss of productivity
- At long-term follow-up, 34.9% were receiving disability benefits
- Although these injuries are rare, occurring at a rate of 0.08% and 0.25%, the impact on patients is profound

---

## Biliary Injury: Intraoperative Cholangiography

- Intraoperative cholangiography has been proposed to reduce iatrogenic bile duct injury during laparoscopic cholecystectomy
- Recent retrospective studies show a higher incidence of CBDI when intraoperative cholangiogram is performed (0.25% vs. 0.12%)
- This is likely because cholangiography is used more frequently during challenging cases

---

## Biliary Injury: Cholangiography Limitations

- Proper biliary anatomy identification and interpretation of the cholangiography images are required for it to aid in prevention of CBDI
- The CVS remains the current standard technique to reduce the incidence of CBDI during cholecystectomy
- Cholangiography is an adjunct, not a replacement for proper anatomical dissection

---

## Biliary Injury: Inflammation Risk

- Inflammation of the gallbladder increases the risk of CBDI
- As the grade of cholecystitis severity increases, the risk of CBDI rises
- Severe inflammation distorts anatomy and makes identification of structures difficult

---

## Figure 36.10: Pathogenesis of the "Classic" Injury

- **Step 1**: The common bile duct is mistaken as the cystic duct and is clipped and divided
- **Step 2**: The dissection is carried up along the left side of the common hepatic duct in the belief that this is the underside of the gallbladder
- **Step 3**: The common hepatic duct is transected while the surgeon tries to dissect what they believe is the gallbladder from the liver bed

---

## Figure 36.10: Classic Injury Mechanism

- If the structure is recognized as a bile duct at this point, it is often thought to be a second cystic duct or an accessory duct
- While the common hepatic duct is divided, the right hepatic artery is often injured
- This creates a combined vasculobiliary injury with severe consequences

---

## Biliary Injury: Classic Injury Cause

- The "classic injury" occurs when the CBD is mistaken for the cystic duct and ligated
- This is thought to occur when the gallbladder is retracted too aggressively to the right
- This causes the cystic duct to lie parallel and adjacent to the CBD

---

## Biliary Injury: Proximal Extension

- Dissection is then continued along the CBD superiorly until an "aberrant" or "duplicated" duct is encountered
- If this duct is subsequently divided, a more proximal bile duct injury will occur
- This extends the damage and complicates subsequent repair

---

## Biliary Injury: Intraoperative Recognition

- If a CBDI is identified at the time of surgery, the surgeon must assess:
  - The extent of the injury
  - Their own experience repairing these injuries
  - The patient's condition
  - The hospital resources

---

## Biliary Injury: Specialist Consultation

- A hepatobiliary surgeon should be called to assess the situation if one is available
- When a specialist is not available, the best course of action is to place a drain near the porta hepatis
- Close the patient, and initiate transfer to a center with hepatobiliary expertise

---

## Biliary Injury: Intraoperative Management

- Proceeding with gallbladder extraction after identifying a biliary injury is not recommended
- This risks amplifying the injury
- Early recognition and appropriate management are critical for optimal outcomes

---

## Biliary Injury: Postoperative Discovery

- CBDIs are often not discovered during the index procedure
- Patients with ongoing abdominal pain, fevers, or ileus should alert the surgeon to a potential complication
- The initial diagnostic test should start with abdominal ultrasound

---

## Biliary Injury: Diagnostic Workup

- Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen should be performed if a complication is suspected
- If excessive peritoneal fluid is present, percutaneous drainage should be performed
- The type of injury should be determined next

---

## Biliary Injury: Defining the Injury

- This can be done with:
  - Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
  - Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
  - Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
- Accurate characterization guides treatment selection

---

## Biliary Injury: Treatment of Simple Leaks

- Simple postoperative leaks can be managed with drainage alone
- Drainage and ERCP placement of biliary stents is another option
- Several centers with advanced gastroenterologists are beginning to manage selected patients with complex injuries with percutaneous-endoscopic rendezvous procedures with promising long-term results

---

## Immediate Postoperative Complications: Bleeding

- Clinically significant bleeding occurs in 0.1% to 1.9% of laparoscopic cholecystectomies
- Bleeding can arise from:
  1. The liver
  2. An abdominal arterial source
  3. Port sites

---

## Bleeding: Liver Bed Sources

- Significant bleeding from the liver bed tends to be from the terminal branches of the middle hepatic vein
- Bleeding from the gallbladder fossa that appears venous in nature can be controlled laparoscopically with hemostatic agents and applied pressure
- Visualization can be improved by lifting the liver and increasing the pressure of pneumoperitoneum

---

## Bleeding: Laparoscopic Control

- Clips or sutures can be placed in the cystic plate for hemostasis if all landmarks are identified
- This avoids injury to underlying portal structures
- If visualization is lost, pressure should be applied to the area with sponge and grasper while converting to laparotomy

---

## Bleeding: Open Management

- During laparotomy, one should keep pressure on the venous injury
- Air embolus is possible and can be severe
- Acute hemodynamic decline in the postoperative period should raise concern for significant bleeding, which is likely because of a dislodged clip

---

## Bleeding: Trocar Site Bleeding

- As with any laparoscopic procedure, bleeding can occur from trocar sites
- Careful trocar placement and inspection at the end of the case can identify these injuries
- Angioembolization may be needed for significant trocar site vascular injuries

---

## Immediate Postoperative Complications: Retained CBD Stones

- Common bile duct stones are present in approximately 5% to 15% of patients presenting for cholecystectomy
- Those suspected of having choledocholithiasis should undergo preoperative diagnostic MRCP or ERCP
- This is especially important if the surgeon is not comfortable exploring the CBD laparoscopically

---

## Retained CBD Stones: Management Approach

- Choledocholithiasis is not an indication for laparotomy in the modern era
- Laparoscopic bile duct exploration at the time of cholecystectomy has been shown to reduce hospital LOS and overall cost compared with endoscopic treatment followed by cholecystectomy
- Retained common duct stones after cholecystectomy are rare

---

## Retained CBD Stones: Incidence and Diagnosis

- In one single center study, the incidence of postoperative ERCP for suspected retained stones was 1.8%
- Those suspected of having a retained CBD stone should be studied with either MRCP or ERCP depending on facility capabilities
- Endoscopic sphincteroplasty with stone extraction is the most widely accepted treatment for this condition in the current era

---

## Immediate Postoperative Complications: Gallbladder Perforation

- Entering the gallbladder during cholecystectomy is a common event
- This occurs particularly during the learning phase of the procedure
- Careful retraction is essential because spillage of bile and stones can result in serious complications

---

## Gallbladder Perforation: Consequences

- Intraperitoneal spillage of stones can lead to abscess and fistula formation
- In patients with incidental gallbladder carcinoma, bile spillage at the time of cholecystectomy resulted in higher rates of carcinomatosis (24% vs. 4%) compared with those without spillage
- Bile spillage is also associated with poorer disease-free survival in incidental gallbladder cancer

---

## Delayed Complications: Remnant Gallbladder and Cystic Duct Stones

- Recurrent stone formation in a remnant gallbladder or cystic duct is rare
- Most patients present with pain similar to their precholecystectomy symptoms
- It can occur at any time from 4 months to 25 years after surgery

---

## Remnant Gallbladder Stones: Associations

- Remnant gallbladder stones are usually associated with subtotal cholecystectomy
- Diagnosis requires a study that delineates the biliary anatomy, such as MRCP or ERCP
- Endoscopic ultrasound, intraoperative cholangiogram, and percutaneous transhepatic cholangiogram can also be useful in obtaining a diagnosis of retained stones

---

## Remnant Gallbladder Stones: Treatment

- Treatment of cystic duct stones can be managed in a variety of ways
- Some stones are amenable to endoscopic retrieval or lithotripsy
- Others require a surgical intervention to extract the stone and ligate the cystic duct closer to the common duct

---

## Remnant Gallbladder: Treatment

- Treatment of a remnant gallbladder typically requires resection to prevent further stone formation
- Depending on the situation and surgeon skill set, completion cholecystectomy can be performed either open or laparoscopically with low morbidity
- Proper preoperative imaging is essential for surgical planning

---

## Delayed Complications: Biliary Strictures

- Benign strictures of the CBD occur in up to 2.7% of laparoscopic cholecystectomies and 0.5% of open cholecystectomies
- These strictures arise from an injury to the bile duct that was unidentified in the immediate postoperative period
- Causes include incomplete transection, clipping or ligation, thermal injury, or ischemic devascularization of the bile duct

---

## Biliary Strictures: Presentation

- Commonly, patients with benign biliary strictures present with symptoms consistent with obstructive jaundice
- These may include:
  - Progressive jaundice
  - Pruritus
  - Dark urine
  - Pale stools
  - Elevated liver enzymes

---

## Biliary Strictures: Endoscopic Management

- Endoscopic treatment is typically the first approach
- Surgery is reserved for those who do not respond to endoscopic therapy
- Endoscopic stenting has been shown to result in 67% of patients being symptom-free for 28 months
- Having a normal ERCP after stenting was predictive of not reforming a stricture

---

## Biliary Strictures: Surgical Management

- Surgery remains the mainstay of therapy for benign biliary strictures after cholecystectomy
- A recent meta-analysis showed that a surgical approach had an 84% long-term patency rate
- The choice between endoscopic and surgical management depends on stricture characteristics and patient factors

---

## Delayed Complications: Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea

- Postcholecystectomy diarrhea is defined as three or more loose stools per day after removal of the gallbladder
- It is difficult to assess the prevalence of this disorder
- Etiology is likely multifactorial in nature

---

## Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea: Pathophysiology

- One factor may be the increased number of bile salts in the colon because of continuous bile flow into the gut
- This leads to secretory diarrhea
- Recent evidence showed that the gut microbiome of patients with postcholecystectomy diarrhea is altered

---

## Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea: Microbiome Findings

- Compared with healthy patients, patients with diarrhea after cholecystectomy had significantly higher levels of Proteobacteria
- These bacteria may be pathogenic in this process
- The role of microbiome modulation in treatment is an area of active research

---

## Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea: Treatment

- Currently, the recommended therapy is the administration of bile-acid binding agents and antidiarrheals
- These have variable success rates
- Dietary modifications may also be helpful in some patients
- Refractory cases may require specialist gastroenterology consultation

---

## Conclusion: Gold Standard

- Cholecystectomy remains the gold standard for the management of gallbladder disease in the developed world
- The vast majority are now performed minimally invasively with excellent results
- Most patients now undergo this operation in an ambulatory setting

---

## Conclusion: Technological Advances

- Attempts at improving outcomes from laparoscopic cholecystectomy will continue to drive the development of novel surgical tools and techniques
- Although relatively safe, there is room to reduce the number of CBDIs
- These injuries have a significant impact on patient quality of life and overall survival

---

## Conclusion: Education and Safety

- These gains will be achieved with improved outreach and education regarding the CVS
- Knowing when to pursue alternative procedures instead of forging ahead with total cholecystectomy is essential
- As new technology arises, surgeons must always keep in mind the safety of the patient alongside the development of new techniques

---

## Conclusion: Key Takeaways

- Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the standard of care
- Critical View of Safety is essential for preventing bile duct injuries
- Subtotal cholecystectomy is a safe alternative when anatomy is unclear
- Conversion to open is a sign of mature surgical judgment, not failure
- Long-term complications, though rare, can significantly impact patient quality of life
